markets.title: How Do We Keep AI Helpful and Honest This Week

paragraphs.text: This morning a note described a new way to manage Meta ads via an AI assistant that asks permission before changes, aiming to keep routines predictable and save time.
Parks says students should drive AI use by comparing tools, reviewing outputs, and setting class rules with input, so learning remains the focus.
A university center in China seeks AI guided drug discovery by looping predictions into experiments to test candidates, aiming for faster insight with verifiable steps.
Paris and Quebec researchers launch an AI lab to study infectious diseases, hoping to spot signs and improve predictions, not promise fast breakthroughs.
A contributor argues that safety requires ongoing checks and independent oversight, not a single test, to prevent drift as capabilities grow.

research.title: What makes a forecast useful?

paragraphs.text: A forecast is only as useful as the test behind it. Two new preprints look at prediction in very different settings and show why the comparison matters.

In a study of next-day stock market forecasts, researchers compared several models with a simple prediction: tomorrow’s closing price will match today’s. In their tests, the models’ average errors did not beat that baseline. The finding concerns the S&P 500 and the data and target studied; it does not settle how models perform on other assets.

A study of tropical cyclones found that adding forecasters’ written discussions to numerical data reduced average wind-speed error in one historical comparison. The researchers caution that their data and timing do not represent a real-time forecasting test.
Together, the papers invite a practical question: does a more elaborate approach improve a meaningful comparison under the conditions where it will be used?
